egypt_status.historical_report: A 1983 USAID-supported maize-virus proceedings volume states that maize streak virus disease was found on maize in Egypt and reports serological, electron-microscopy, and leafhopper-transmission identification involving Cicadulina bipunctella zeae.
egypt_status.modern_evidence_caution: The located Egyptian field-survey literature from 2004–2005 primarily documents Maize Yellow Stripe Virus (MYSV), a different leafhopper-borne virus in the genus Tenuivirus, not MSV. No recent Egypt-specific molecular survey confirming MSV was located.
egypt_status.confidence: Historical Egypt occurrence is documented, but current national prevalence and the identity of contemporary Egyptian streak-like symptoms remain uncertain.

early_stage: Minute pale green, white, or yellow circular flecks on the youngest newly expanding leaves
Flecks may initially be 0.5–2 mm and difficult to see without close inspection
characteristic_leaf_symptoms: Narrow broken or continuous chlorotic streaks running parallel to leaf veins
Streaks are commonly more visible along secondary and tertiary veins than the midrib
Streaks may fuse laterally into longer yellow or white stripes
Some isolates or host responses can produce red or reddish pigmentation
whole_plant_symptoms: Shortened leaves and reduced plant height
Severe stunting when infection occurs before the 4–5 leaf stage
Shortened internodes and weak or abnormal growth
Small, misshapen, poorly filled, or absent ears
Possible abnormal bunching of shoots or flowers in some grass hosts
image_annotation_targets: pale flecks on newly emerged leaves
streak orientation parallel to secondary and tertiary veins
whole-plant height compared with healthy plants

symptom_colors: red or reddish in some isolates
distribution_on_plant: Symptoms occur primarily on leaves that emerge after infection; older leaves formed before infection may remain healthy. Streaks extend along secondary and tertiary veins and can cover most of newly formed leaves in severe cases.
affected_parts: ears/cobs indirectly through stunting and reproductive failure
progression: The leafhopper introduces the virus during feeding.
Tiny pale flecks appear on the youngest leaves formed after infection.
Flecks elongate along secondary and tertiary veins into broken yellow or white streaks.
Streaks merge and may extend over much of each new leaf.
Early infection causes severe stunting, shortened leaves, and possible plant death.
Surviving plants may produce small, misshapen, poorly filled, or barren ears.

vector_and_transmission.egypt_historical_vector_report: Cicadulina bipunctella zeae was reported in the historical Egypt MSV account.
vector_and_transmission.transmission: Persistent leafhopper transmission; the virus can also be maintained in infected grass hosts and maize volunteers.
vector_and_transmission.important_differential_vector: Egyptian MYSV field studies identify Cicadulina chinai as the vector of MYSV, not proof of MSV transmission.

egypt_field_context.historical_record: The Egypt MSV report is associated with virus-disease work presented in 1982/1983 proceedings.
egypt_field_context.current_surveillance_gap: No recent Egypt-wide MSV incidence map, sequence dataset, or confirmed Egyptian MSV strain record was located in the search.
egypt_field_context.related_egyptian_virus: Maize Yellow Stripe Virus has been surveyed in Lower and Middle Egypt and causes yellow stripes, smaller leaves, stunting, and curved apical leaves; it must be separated from MSV by serology or molecular diagnosis.

environment.temperature: MSV epidemiology is influenced by temperature, rainfall, drought, and leafhopper population dynamics; no Egypt-specific MSV temperature threshold was located.
environment.rainfall: Drought followed by irregular rain can favour leafhopper movement and epidemic development in African MSV systems; this is general epidemiological evidence, not an Egypt-specific threshold.
environment.crop_calendar: Overlapping or staggered maize and grass production can maintain virus and vectors between crops.
environment.grass_hosts: Wild and cultivated grasses can act as virus or vector reservoirs.

similar_diseases.name: Maize Yellow Stripe Virus
similar_diseases.pathogen: Maize yellow stripe virus, genus Tenuivirus
similar_diseases.egypt_relevance: Confirmed in Egyptian surveys of Middle and Lower Egypt.
similar_diseases.visual_difference: Can cause yellow stripes, smaller leaves, stunting, and curved apical leaves; visual separation from MSV is unreliable, so ELISA, RT-PCR, or hybridization is needed.

similar_diseases.name: Maize Mosaic Virus
similar_diseases.visual_difference: Often produces mosaic or mottled patterns and stunting rather than the fine, vein-parallel streaks characteristic of MSV.

similar_diseases.name: Maize Chlorotic Stunt or Dwarf Diseases
similar_diseases.pathogen: Virus or mollicute complexes depending on disease designation
similar_diseases.visual_difference: Stunting and chlorosis can be prominent, but confirmation requires laboratory testing because symptoms overlap with MSV and MYSV.

similar_diseases.name: Nutrient deficiency or herbicide injury
similar_diseases.visual_difference: May cause generalized chlorosis or striping but lacks confirmed leafhopper transmission and virus-specific laboratory signals.

diagnostic_caution: MSV cannot be confirmed reliably from symptoms alone in Egypt because MYSV and other maize virus-like diseases produce overlapping yellow stripes and stunting. Use ELISA, PCR/RT-PCR, hybridization, electron microscopy, and vector transmission tests as appropriate.

research_notes: This record distinguishes historical MSV evidence from modern Egyptian evidence for MYSV. A current Egyptian sample with streaking should not be labelled MSV without laboratory confirmation.
